finding.claim: dropTable ignores the error returned by Authorize, so the authorization check is not enforced. Any request that reaches the handler executes DROP TABLE, whether or not the user has the dba role.
finding.source: Any authenticated HTTP user, with any roles, sending a request to /admin/drop with form value t.
finding.sink: runSQL("DROP TABLE " + r.FormValue("t")) at api.go:27, a destructive admin operation.

trace.note: /admin/drop is registered to dropTable with no middleware.
userFrom(r) fetches the user from the request context.
Authorize(u, "dba") returns errors.New("forbidden") for non-dba users, but the return value is discarded.
Execution continues to runSQL regardless of the authorization result.

finding.guards_checked: The only guard is Authorize at line 26, and its result is ignored. The route is registered with no auth middleware in main. The sibling handler vacuum checks the error correctly, which shows the check was intended here.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 is the only guard. It returns an error, but the call is a bare statement and the result is discarded. No middleware is registered at api.go:44. The sibling vacuum handler at api.go:33 tests the error correctly.
verdict.reason: api.go:26 discards the error from Authorize, so api.go:27 runs `DROP TABLE` with the unsanitized `t` form value for any user, dba or not. One caveat: nothing in this directory sets the "user" context value (the only match is the read at api.go:22). As written, the type assertion at api.go:22 panics on a nil value before line 26. The bug is reachable once any external layer puts a *User in the request context.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 returns an error for non-dba users, but the call is a bare statement and the result is discarded. No middleware wraps the route at api.go:44. The sibling vacuum handler tests the error at api.go:33.
verdict_facts.reason: At api.go:26 the error from Authorize is discarded, so api.go:27 runs DROP TABLE with the user-supplied table name for any authenticated user regardless of role, and the route at api.go:44 has no other check.

finding.claim: SQL injection: the attacker-controlled form value t is concatenated directly into a DROP TABLE statement with no validation or identifier quoting. Even a legitimate dba caller can inject arbitrary SQL, and with F1 any user can.
finding.source: r.FormValue("t"), which reads the query string or POST body of /admin/drop.
finding.sink: runSQL("DROP TABLE " + t) at api.go:27, which executes SQL. The stub body is empty, but the call is clearly intended as a SQL executor.

trace.note: r.FormValue("t") is concatenated into the SQL string.
runSQL takes the raw string. The stub has no parameterization or allowlist.

finding.guards_checked: No allowlist of table names, no identifier quoting, and no regex validation. DDL identifiers cannot be bound as parameters, so an allowlist is required, and none exists.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 returns an error, but the result is discarded as a bare statement, so it blocks nothing. There is no allowlist, quoting or validation on t. The only comparable check is vacuum's tested Authorize at api.go:33, which is a different handler.
verdict.reason: api.go:27 concatenates r.FormValue("t") into "DROP TABLE " and passes it to runSQL (a stub at api.go:41, plainly meant as a SQL executor). The only guard, Authorize at api.go:26, has its error discarded, so any authenticated user reaches the sink. Because the sink is an empty stub, the injection is confirmed by intent rather than by observed execution.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 is a bare statement with its error discarded, so it does not block. No allowlist, quoting or validation exists.
verdict_facts.reason: api.go:27 concatenates r.FormValue("t") into the SQL passed to runSQL (api.go:41, an empty stub standing in for the executor), and the only guard at api.go:26 discards its result, so any authenticated user can inject SQL (the "even a dba" part adds little, since dba already holds DROP power).

finding.claim: userFrom does an unchecked type assertion on the context value. If no authentication middleware has set the "user" key, the assertion panics. Both routes are registered with no auth middleware, so unauthenticated requests hit this path. net/http recovers the panic per request, so this is a limited issue. It also means the code has no real authentication, so anonymous access is only blocked by the panic.
finding.sink: r.Context().Value("user").(*User), which panics on a nil interface value.

trace.note: Route registered with no authentication wrapper.
The single-value type assertion panics when the value is missing.

finding.guards_checked: No authentication middleware exists in this file. If the middleware lives elsewhere, the panic is not reachable. The lone api.go has no such middleware, so this is low confidence and mostly a robustness issue.

verdict.guard_found: none: no auth middleware exists, but the panic at api.go:22 aborts the handler before any effect, and net/http recovers it per request.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (api.go:22 does the unchecked assertion and api.go:44-45 register the routes with no wrapper), but an anonymous request panics at api.go:25 and api.go:32 before runSQL (api.go:27, 37), so nothing runs and the only effect is a recovered per-request panic, which is a robustness issue and not an exploitable vulnerability.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Upstream trusted middleware (per project facts) populates the "user" context value before these handlers run. Within api.go, Authorize at line 33 gates vacuum. dropTable discards the Authorize result at line 26.
verdict_facts.reason: The trace lines are accurate (api.go:22 is an unchecked assertion, api.go:44 registers the route bare), but the maintainer states that upstream middleware, outside this directory, sets the context user, so the panic at api.go:22 is not reachable by an anonymous request and nothing is bypassed. The real flaw in this file is different: dropTable ignores Authorize's return value at api.go:26, so any authenticated user can run the DROP, and the table name from r.FormValue("t") is concatenated into the SQL. That belongs in its own finding and is not what F3 claims.
